analysis.one_liner: Raises federal taxes on snuff and chewing tobacco to match cigarette taxes and funds anti-tobacco education.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise smokeless tobacco taxes and fund public education never got a vote; it sat in two House committees until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal excise tax on snuff from 36 cents to $4.25 per pound and on chewing tobacco from 12 cents to $1.12 per pound, bringing smokeless tobacco taxation roughly in line with cigarettes, with automatic adjustments if cigarette taxes rise again [S3]. Ten percent of the new revenue would fund a new trust fund for public education about the risks of smokeless tobacco and programs to reduce its use; the other 90 percent would go to general federal revenue [S3]. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees in November 1995 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People deterred from starting or continuing smokeless tobacco use — historically a habit concentrated among young men and rural communities — gain lower disease risk as higher prices discourage consumption. Public health programs gain a dedicated funding stream, and the general Treasury gains revenue [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people and rural tobacco users

how_it_helps.text: Raises the snuff tax from 36 cents to $4.25 per pound and the chewing tobacco tax from 12 cents to $1.12 per pound, matching the structure of cigarette taxation [S3].
Ties smokeless tobacco tax rates to future increases in the cigarette tax, so the gap cannot quietly reopen [S3].

Creates a Smokeless Tobacco Education and Prevention Trust Fund, seeded with 10 percent of the net new revenue, to pay for public education about smokeless tobacco risks and programs to reduce consumption [S2].

Imposes a one-time tax on existing wholesale inventory ($3.87 per pound of snuff, $1.00 per pound of chewing tobacco) so stocks can't be stockpiled tax-free before the increase, while exempting retail shelves [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who use snuff and chewing tobacco would pay much higher prices — a regressive burden falling on a user base that skews rural and working-class. Smokeless tobacco manufacturers would absorb a roughly twelve-fold tax increase on snuff, hitting sales; wholesalers holding inventory would owe the one-time floor stocks tax [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Snuff and chewing tobacco users and makers

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes fall hardest on people who keep using the product by choice, and smokeless tobacco users skew rural and lower-income, so the cost is regressive [S3].
Only 10 percent of the new revenue goes to the education fund; the remaining 90 percent is general federal revenue, so the health-program funding is modest relative to the tax burden [S3].
The one-time floor stocks tax and immediate effective date would impose upfront compliance costs on wholesalers and manufacturers holding inventory at enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanism is well established: higher tobacco prices reduce use, especially among young people, and this bill closes a real gap in which snuff and chewing tobacco were taxed at a tiny fraction of the cigarette rate while carrying serious oral-cancer risks. The honest costs are a regressive price increase on adults who use the product by choice and the fact that most of the money raised goes to general revenue rather than to health programs. On balance the benefits to public health outweigh the costs, though the bill's design gives more to the Treasury than to prevention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees in November 1995, and one of them sent it to a subcommittee, but neither committee ever acted on it, so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Patricia Schroeder and 7 original cosponsors introduced the bill on November 6, 1995 [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has jurisdiction over tobacco taxes, and to the Commerce Committee [S5].
On November 20, 1995 it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for either committee [S5].
The bill attracted 26 cosponsors, 24 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but never advanced beyond referral before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Smokeless tobacco manufacturers kept selling at the old 36-cent and 12-cent tax rates, and their customers kept paying the old prices, because the tax increase never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Smokeless tobacco makers and their customers

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so opposition never took a recorded form; the only measurable support was bipartisan in sponsorship, with 24 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: A roughly twelve-fold increase in the snuff tax and a nine-fold increase on chewing tobacco would have sharply raised prices and cut sales. The industry profits from a product with serious oral-health risks, so its interest in the bill ran directly against the public health goal.
Lower manufacturer sales mean less demand for leaf, and the one-time floor stocks tax falls on inventory held by wholesalers and warehouses at enactment.
Higher prices would reduce sales volume, though the bill exempts retail shelf stock from the one-time inventory tax.
